source.title: Scaling up the State Size of RNN LLMs for Long-Context Scenarios
source.authors: Kai Liu; Jian-Fei Gao; Kai Chen

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as background, but studies scaling RNN state size and its effects on recall—not the loss, parameter/token/compute laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-modeling and downstream benchmark scores for state-size variants, but does not fit or test the listed scaling-law claims. It explicitly describes its analysis as a coarse state-size scaling trend rather than a precise scaling-law analysis. The reported benchmark scores are not rows for V6 because they do not test downstream predictability from model scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The paper scales RNN state size and measures recall-context length and benchmark scores. It fits no loss power law in parameters, tokens or compute, attempts no extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation, and does not test downstream predictability from scale or loss. Scaling laws appear only as background in Section 2.2 and the Limitations, where the authors say they did not attempt a precise scaling-law analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that scaling RNN state size improves long-context and recall ability, with recall context length growing nearly linearly with state size. They explicitly defer a precise scaling-law analysis to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper scales RNN state size and measures recall-context trends; it does not use the original works' held-out-loss curve fitting or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that long-context evaluation is sensitive to evaluation methods, training data, and prompts. The recall-context plots also vary the accuracy threshold and, for the 1.5B models, needle type.

fits_no_version.finding: Maximum recall context length on S-NIAH grows near-linearly with RNN state-size expansion. Gated DeltaNet has a steeper slope than GLA, and the 1.5B trend matches the 400M one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For linear-attention RNNs, expanding recurrent state size increases maximum recallable context length roughly linearly, with a slope that depends on the update rule.

fits_no_version.finding: At roughly matched parameter counts (about 455M or 1.68B), scaling layers (-L) and scaling state size (-E8) give similar Wikitext perplexity: GLA 25.41 vs 25.99, Gated DeltaNet 400M 24.17 vs 23.61, Gated DeltaNet 1.5B 16.42 vs 15.66. The recall gains differ much more.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Allocating parameters to recurrent state size rather than depth changes LM perplexity little at fixed parameters but changes recall ability substantially.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The authors state that they do not conduct a precise scaling-law analysis, citing evaluation sensitivity and the limited number of experiments possible because large-state RNN training is slow. The recall-context trend values are presented in figures without exact numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Language-modeling and downstream benchmark scores in Tables 3–5, including aggregate retrieval and LongBench results, are not extracted: they compare state-size variants but do not test any listed version's loss-scaling law or downstream predictability claim.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss power law in N, D or C is fitted.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
Depth/width at fixed parameters is not studied as such. Only a layers-vs-state-size comparison at matched parameters is reported (Table 3); see notes.
All: only text LM pretraining is studied, and no power-law form is fitted.
All: downstream scores are compared across variants but not predicted from scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 3 layers-vs-state comparison at matched parameters is loosely V4-adjacent: it shows small perplexity differences from an architecture choice. However, it is not a depth/width shape sweep, it covers only two points per model, and it does not report loss as a function of shape. It is therefore recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a V4 test. Rows R1–R10 are correctly unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Loss sensitivity to depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from model scale or pretraining loss; the paper reports state-size comparisons, not such a predictive relationship.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
